clue.text: One bites firm end of fig

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of fig

explanation.surface: Someone takes a bite from the hard tip of a fig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One bites' looks like a person eating; it is the definition, since a gear tooth bites into the next wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A cog is a tooth on a gear wheel, and its teeth are said to bite or engage with another wheel.

clue.text: Heating stoked coal on one fire almost turning cold

indicators.note: turning round sends the letters back the other way
stoking a fire stirs it up, so the letters are stirred into a new order
almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be stirred
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, then cut short
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone stokes a coal fire that is almost dying as the weather turns cold.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the stirred coal above the rest. One plus FIR (fire without its last letter) is turned round to give RIFI, and C ends it: CALORIFIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Calorific means producing heat, so as an adjective it can stand for heating, as in heating power.

clue.text: Sauce made from fish and … um … that's it

definitions.text: Sauce made from fish and … um … that's it

parts.note: a gar is a long-snouted fish
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook stumbles over the recipe for a sauce: fish and, um, nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer and also builds it: a fish followed by the hesitation. Garum was the fermented fish sauce of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Garum was a Roman condiment made by fermenting fish in salt, so a sauce with fish as its main ingredient.

clue.text: Old ripe bananas with decent chopped nuts getting tasted

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: going bananas means going crazy, so the letters are thrown into disorder
nuts means mad, so these letters are scrambled too
something chopped has had a piece cut off its end

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written, then cut and rearranged

explanation.surface: Old ripe bananas and some good chopped nuts are being sampled.
explanation.walkthrough: The food words are all instructions: 'bananas' and 'nuts' both mean crazy, and 'chopped' removes the final T of decent.
explanation.definitionFit: To have tasted something is to have experienced it, as in 'tasted defeat'; both are past participles.

clue.text: Endless roulade, initially eaten in a frenzy, then left

indicators.note: then signals the next piece is added at the end of what came before
something eaten goes inside, so the first letter sits within the jumble
a frenzy is wild disorder, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the opening letter of roulade
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A roulade was wolfed down in a frenzy and nothing was left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eaten' does double duty: its letters are the jumbled fodder, and being eaten means the R goes inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal describes something without end, a direct synonym of endless.

clue.text: Show-off that's more 'sophisticated' rejecting last bit of sandwich

indicators.note: rejecting something means throwing it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: posh means sophisticated, so more of it is the comparative; the answer also runs backwards across these words, a coincidence the setter did not intend

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of sandwich

explanation.surface: A show-off turns down the dregs of a sandwich because it is beneath them.
explanation.walkthrough: The H from the end of sandwich is removed from POSHER.
explanation.definitionFit: A poser is a person who strikes attitudes to impress others, the same as a show-off.

clue.text: Judges drunk by about 1:50 in Reading

indicators.note: taken in alongside, so the following piece is placed next to what comes before it

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a judge hears a case in court
one is a, as in a single thing
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Judges are drunk by ten to two in the Berkshire town of Reading.
explanation.walkthrough: '1:50' looks like a time but splits into two numbers. Reading here is a run-through of a play, not the town west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice performance, and a read-through of a script is called a reading.

clue.text: The last ice-cream portion is bigger, potentially

indicators.note: a portion is a piece of something, so the answer is a part of the run of words

parts.note: found across the end of the first word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: The final helping of ice cream looks like it might be the largest.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a playful description of something that can be stretched.
explanation.definitionFit: An elastic thing can stretch, so it can potentially become bigger than it is.

clue.text: Is it used to eat Chinese pork? Yes

definitions.text: Is it used to eat Chinese
definitions.note: phrased as a question; the answer is the thing used

parts.note: pork chops are cuts of pork
a tick is the mark that says yes on a form

explanation.surface: A diner asks whether pork is eaten with a Chinese utensil and is told yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads as one sentence, but its first half is the definition and the reply gives the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A chopstick is one of a pair of slender sticks used for eating East Asian food.

clue.text: Mess up the topping for summer puddings

parts.note: to duff something is to bungle it

indicators.note: the topping of a word in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of summer

explanation.surface: Someone ruins the cream topping on a batch of summer puddings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer puddings' reads as a dessert name, but the definition is just puddings. A duff is a boiled suet pudding, as in plum duff.
explanation.definitionFit: Duff is a traditional British boiled or steamed suet pudding, so duffs are puddings of that kind.

clue.text: Stores delivering Russian cars

indicators.note: delivering a speech means saying it out loud, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: Ladas are cars made in Russia

explanation.surface: Shops are taking delivery of cars from Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound match relies on a British accent, where the R in the middle is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a cool room or cupboard where food is kept, so larders are food stores.

clue.text: Leave some lettuce on? No

parts.note: a head of lettuce is a single whole one
the opposite of on

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to put lettuce in a sandwich and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like 'leave it on', but it is a verb meaning depart.
explanation.definitionFit: To head off is a phrasal verb for setting out or departing, which is to leave.

clue.text: Dish made by male artists?

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
men are males

explanation.surface: A meal is cooked by a group of male painters.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'male artists' is to be read as RA men, Academicians who are men.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup served in a bowl, so it is a dish in the culinary sense.

clue.text: Broken by bread, ultimately toaster fails special checks

indicators.note: a thing broken by another has that other pushed into its middle
a machine that fails has gone wrong, so its letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end of the word, its final letter

parts.note: the closing letter of bread
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A toaster wrecked by a jammed slice of bread fails its safety inspections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'special checks' looks like one phrase, but S for special is wordplay and the definition is just checks.
explanation.definitionFit: Road tests are trials of a vehicle or product under real conditions, a kind of check on performance.

clue.text: Trucks by which spaghetti's eaten?

parts.note: surface reading: lorries, with the odd suggestion of eating pasta with a vehicle
setter's reading: the action of raising pasta on a fork, split into two words

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into fork and lifts: what you do to spaghetti. As one word it names warehouse vehicles with prongs.
explanation.definitionFit: Forklifts are small industrial trucks with prongs at the front for raising pallets.

clue.text: Have a go at and complain — it's a British tradition

parts.note: to roast someone is to criticise them harshly
to beef is slang for to grumble

explanation.surface: Grumbling and griping at others is presented as a national custom.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sunday roast of beef is so associated with England that the French nickname the English les rosbifs.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast beef with Yorkshire pudding is the classic English Sunday lunch, a long-standing national custom.

clue.text: The natural order of things in Iceland?

definitions.text: The natural order of things in Iceland?

parts.note: surface reading: the ecological ranking of who eats whom, set in the Nordic country
setter's reading: Iceland is a British supermarket business with many branches selling frozen groceries

explanation.walkthrough: Iceland is a UK retailer specialising in frozen groceries, so it is a chain that sells things to eat; the ecological sense supplies 'natural order'.
explanation.definitionFit: In ecology the phrase names the sequence of organisms each feeding on the next, a natural hierarchy.

clue.text: Side of letter I forgot to write

parts.note: chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a postscript adds what the writer forgot to put in the letter

explanation.surface: A letter writer adds a note on the side about something they forgot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' and 'Side' both suggest correspondence, but side is a side order at a meal; chips are fries.
explanation.definitionFit: Chips (fries) are a typical side dish ordered alongside a main course.

clue.text: Given too much seafood? Finally, the diet is abandoned!

parts.note: surf is the sea half of surf and turf, a seafood and steak dish

indicators.note: abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose
finally points to the closing letter of the next word

parts.note: the closing letter of the
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stuffed with seafood announces that the diet is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that surf is only food by way of the dish surf and turf.
explanation.definitionFit: To be surfeited is to have been fed or supplied to excess, so given too much.

clue.text: American guy crosses river and leaves

indicators.note: to cross something here is to straddle it, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: Chad is a common American man's name
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An American man crosses a river and then goes away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' reads as a verb after 'and', but it is the noun: chard is grown for its leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Chard is a leafy vegetable whose large green leaves are eaten, so it is leaves in the greengrocer's sense.

clue.text: Where one might eat catch taken in by high tide

indicators.note: something taken in is held inside, so one piece goes within the other
high can mean intoxicated, so the letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
to net is to catch

explanation.surface: A fisherman's catch is swept up by a high tide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high tide' looks like a fixed phrase, but 'high' is the signal to rearrange tide.
explanation.definitionFit: A dinette is a small dining area or alcove off a kitchen, a place for meals.

clue.text: Spooner's work with butter brand reveals a craft of sorts

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: work is toil; it loses its opening sound to the second word
Anchor is a butter brand sold in Britain; it takes the opening sound of the first word

explanation.surface: Spooner's piece about a butter label turns out to show a sort of handicraft.
explanation.walkthrough: Anchor is a New Zealand butter brand familiar in Britain. 'craft' is not handiwork but a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil tanker is a ship built to carry crude oil, and craft is a general word for a vessel.

clue.text: Soldier on LSD that works to achieve neutrality

parts.note: a soldier is a kind of ant
acid is slang for the drug LSD

explanation.surface: A soldier high on drugs tries to keep the peace between sides.
explanation.walkthrough: Neutrality sounds political, but it is the chemical sense of neither acid nor alkaline.
explanation.definitionFit: An antacid neutralises stomach acid, bringing the pH towards neutral.

clue.text: Former volunteers retired in California, chasing a whiff of flowers?

indicators.note: chasing means following behind, so these pieces come after the opening one

parts.note: BO is body odour, an unpleasant whiff
the TA was the Territorial Army, Britain's former volunteer reserve

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn or gone back, so the short word reads backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then turned back
Cal is an abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: Ex-soldiers retired to California, following the scent of blossoms.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that botanical covers all plants, not just flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanical means relating to plants, and flowers are the showiest plants, so the definition works by example.

clue.text: One-litre bar bottles produced

indicators.note: to bottle something is to shut it inside, so the others go within

parts.note: bar means except, as does but
the Roman numeral for one
L is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: A pub bottles up a single litre of drink it has made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' and 'bottles' make a pub scene, but bar is the preposition meaning except.
explanation.definitionFit: Built means constructed or made, so it can stand for produced.

clue.text: Vanilla Ice samples guitar parts

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tastes of vanilla ice cream taken with the tongue
second meaning: short musical phrases played by a guitarist

explanation.walkthrough: Vanilla Ice is a rapper famous for sampling another song, so the clue reads as music throughout; the first half is really ice cream.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both tongue-tastes of something and short riffs a guitarist plays.

clue.text: Junk that is put on potato in Scotland

parts.note: tat is cheap rubbish
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for that is

explanation.surface: Rubbish is piled onto a potato somewhere in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Scotland' marks the definition as a Scots dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattie or tatie is the Scottish colloquial word for a potato.

clue.text: Weight I put on top of cement mixer

parts.note: a ton is a unit of weight
taken as written

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of cement

explanation.surface: A builder loads a heavy weight on top of a cement mixer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cement mixer' looks like a machine, but mixer stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonic water is a drink commonly added to spirits such as gin, which makes it a mixer.

clue.text: Drink cold water before date, excitedly

indicators.note: before means coming first, so the opening piece leads the rest

parts.note: ice is frozen water

indicators.note: doing something excitedly is agitated, so the letters are stirred up

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone nervously drinks cold water before going on a date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink' looks like a verb, but it is the noun definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Iced tea is chilled tea served as a refreshing cold beverage.

clue.text: Clown enthusiast that mimics a horse

parts.note: Coco was a famous circus clown
a nut is a fan, as in a fitness nut

explanation.surface: A clown who loves horses does impressions of one.
explanation.walkthrough: Half coconut shells clapped together make the sound of hooves, a classic radio and theatre effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Coconut shell halves knocked together imitate hoofbeats, so the coconut is the thing that mimics a horse.

clue.text: Passages coated with brown, sticky stuff beginning to dry, becoming stuck-up

indicators.note: coated with means covered by, so the covering piece goes on the front

parts.note: toffee is a brown, chewy sweet
the nose holds the nasal passages

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of dry

explanation.surface: Pipes coated in a brown, sticky residue start to dry out and get blocked.
explanation.walkthrough: Toffee-nosed is British slang for snobbish. 'stuck-up' looks like it continues the sticky picture but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee-nosed is a British colloquialism for snobbish or haughty, the same as stuck-up.

clue.text: Fish from Marillion's penultimate album's out

indicators.note: the album being out means it sits on the outside, around the other piece

parts.note: a CD is an album on disc

indicators.note: penultimate means next to last, so the second-to-last letter is kept

parts.note: the next-to-last letter of the band's name

explanation.surface: A fish is drawn from Marillion's second-to-last record, which has just been released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'album's out' sounds like a release date; it puts CD around the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cod is a common white sea fish, eaten widely in fish and chips.
